title: Human Bench Network for AI Agents
one_liner: An API-fronted network of laid-off expert bench scientists who run ad hoc wet-lab experiments for AI agents and return machine-readable execution records.
customer: AI-first biotechs, AI-for-science startups and university groups (5-60 people, seed to Series B) that run agent swarms but have no wet lab; later, programs adjacent to frontier labs.
problem: Agent swarms now propose far more experiments than anyone can run. Anthropic's run went from 200,000+ reverse transcriptases to 20 candidates using ~950 agents in 21 hours. Stanford's Virtual Biotech (37,000 agents, Science, Sept 17, 2026) says the next step is testing findings in real labs. Cloud labs and robots handle fixed assays, but not ad hoc molecular biology: Anthropic itself found robotics less conducive to ad hoc workflows and kept human scientists at the bench. Human review and bench work are the bottleneck.
solution: Ticketed experiments through an API or MCP endpoint. The agent proposes a protocol and a senior scientist does feasibility triage. A vetted contractor then runs it at sublet or surplus benches, BSL-1/2 only. Each job returns a signed record that separates AI proposal, human edit and physical execution (deviations, photos, instrument logs, raw data). Fixed price per experiment. Start with commodity molecular biology: cloning, small-scale expression and purification, ELISA/BLI/qPCR, enzyme activity, bacterial and cell-culture assays.
why_now: Frontier labs and Stanford now say publicly that bench execution is the bottleneck. BioSpace tracks 15,000+ biopharma job cuts across 50+ companies in 2026, which supplies skilled hands. The OpenAI Foundation plans to distribute $1B by year-end through Public Data for Health, which creates grant-funded demand for data generation. Lab Manager notes there is no sign-off standard for AI-directed experiments, and this record format supplies one. Anthropic has said it wants to work with other scientists.
revenue_model: $1.5-8k per experiment at roughly 35-45% gross margin, monthly retainers with minimum volumes for agent-heavy customers, and a premium for 48-hour turnaround. The platform keeps a take rate on contractor labor.
non_obvious_insight: Compute is now nearly free compared with bench throughput, and robots failed as the universal answer because real biology is ad hoc. The defensible assets are a pre-vetted pool of humans and a structured execution record that agents can learn from. Humans become the last-mile actuator for AI. Adaptyv and cloud labs cover single fixed assays; nobody sells the long tail of one-off experiments.
first_30_days: Recruit 10-15 laid-off molecular biologists in Boston, SF and San Diego through layoff trackers and alumni groups. Rent 2-3 sublet benches or surplus CRO benches. Define three ticket types with fixed prices. Pitch 10 AI protein-design and agent startups and close 3-5 pilots. Aim for the first 20 paid experiments and publish the sample record schema.

tournament.cluster: Autonomous and AI-directed labs: infrastructure, safety and access
judge_notes: contrarian: rank 5/24 - Humans as last-mile actuators for agents is contrarian and right; idle lab space and laid-off scientists give cheap supply.
operator: rank 6/25 - High ticket per experiment and identifiable AI-biotech buyers, but startups already have CRO options and quality risk is high.
vc: rank 3/25 - Timely: bench execution is now the bottleneck for agent-driven science. Fast to pilot, but it is a services business.

competitors.name: Adaptyv Bio (Adaptyv Biosystems)
competitors.what_they_do: Automated protein-validation lab with an API and an MCP server, so Claude Code or Claude Desktop can order experiments, track them and pull structured results. Assays: binding, expression, thermostability, enzyme activity, plus custom target protein expression. It calls itself 'the automated lab for agentic biology' and plans to add more complex workflows. Customers include AI-first labs Chai Discovery and Boltz as well as Roche and Novo Nordisk. Anthropic ran a protein-design benchmark and competition with it. Docs: https://docs.adaptyvbio.com/llms.txt
competitors.scale_or_funding: $40M Series A (Aug 2026, led by Highland Europe, with Ace Ventures, ByFounders, YC); $8M seed in 2025; 100+ customers; throughput up 5x in a year; staff going from 25 to about 60; capacity to triple by end of 2026. Source: https://www.startupticker.ch/en/news/adaptyv-raises-40m-to-build-automated-lab-for-agentic-biology

competitors.name: Ginkgo Bioworks (Cloud Lab and Datapoints)
competitors.what_they_do: Autonomous cloud lab in Boston that external customers can run experiments on 'virtually', plus Ginkgo Datapoints assay services and open-ended R&D projects. OpenAI's GPT-5 autonomously ran 36,000 cell-free protein synthesis experiments there in a Feb 2026 collaboration (R&D World). Ginkgo staff still prepared reagents and loaded consumables. Benchling one-click ordering now includes Ginkgo alongside Twist and Adaptyv. Ginkgo's Q1 2026 revenue fell and it is restructuring.
competitors.scale_or_funding: Public company; over 130 customers (Novartis, Pfizer, Biogen, Bayer and others)

competitors.name: Emerald Cloud Lab
competitors.what_they_do: Remote-controlled cloud lab with 200+ instrument models. It explicitly supports one-off and ad hoc experiments and design-of-experiments work through a software interface. I found no AI-agent-specific product, and pricing is not public. Its robotics-first approach is the kind Anthropic said suits ad hoc molecular biology less well.
competitors.scale_or_funding: Private and long-established; funding not disclosed on its site

competitors.name: Science Exchange and Scientist.com (CRO marketplaces)
competitors.what_they_do: Marketplaces for contract research. Scientist.com lists 6,000+ pre-qualified providers across 1,000+ categories, with AI-guided intake, auto-negotiation and an average of 1.5 days from request to statement of work (SOW). Science Exchange lists 3,800+ suppliers and offers a Virtual Lab Manager service for small biotechs. Both already sell custom, ad hoc bench work from human CROs, but through quotes and SOWs rather than an agent-callable fixed-price API. I found no public API for either. Science Exchange: https://www.scienceexchange.com
competitors.scale_or_funding: Established. Scientist.com cites $3B+ in procurement activity; Science Exchange cites 3,800+ suppliers. Funding figures not verified.

competitors.name: GenScript, Twist and similar commodity molecular-biology CROs
competitors.what_they_do: Sell exactly the commodity 'long tail' listed in the idea (gene synthesis and cloning, protein expression, antibodies, assay development) with online quick-order tools and fast turnaround, for example 3-7 day harvest. GenScript pitches AI drug discovery solutions that validate in about 4 days. They do not offer an agent API, signed execution records or a per-experiment fixed price for arbitrary protocols.
competitors.scale_or_funding: Large public and established vendors (GenScript is listed in Hong Kong); Twist is a Benchling ordering partner

competitors.name: Transfyr
competitors.what_they_do: Sensor stack and multimodal models that record atomic-action-level execution of lab work, aiming at 'a lossless and unbiased record of scientific execution'. It partners with 'the top frontier AI labs'. It is a capture and provenance layer for human scientists, AI and robots, not a bench-labor network. It could easily supply or compete with the signed execution record.

competitors.name: Medra
competitors.what_they_do: Sells a 'Physical AI Scientist' platform, meaning robotic workcells with natural-language protocol programming and closed-loop optimization. It sells hardware and software to labs, not outsourced experiments. Partners include Genentech and a DARPA-funded collaboration; it launched an AI Experimentalist in June 2026.

competitors.name: Vertically integrated AI-science labs (Lila Sciences, Periodic Labs, Anthropic's own wet lab)
competitors.what_they_do: They build their own labs and do not buy bench capacity. Anthropic's Sept 2026 post confirms all lab work is done by human scientists and that automation is 'less conducive to the sort of ad hoc workflows' in its molecular biology. It also invites outside researchers to send research proposals. That validates the thesis but shows the largest potential buyer is insourcing. Lila and Periodic figures come from Google News RSS results (Bloomberg, TechCrunch, Startup Fortune); I did not open the articles.
competitors.scale_or_funding: Lila Sciences: reported talks at an $8.5B valuation (June 2026), $350M Series A. Periodic Labs: $300M seed, about $7B valuation talks. Anthropic acquired Coefficient Bio for $400M (per a Tekedia headline).

competitors.name: RentAHuman.ai
competitors.what_they_do: General marketplace where AI agents hire humans for physical-world tasks, with proof review and escrow. It has 750k+ registered humans in 100+ countries. It has no lab-science category, but it shows the 'humans as last-mile actuator for agents' framing exists and is funded by attention, so someone could vertically specialize it.
competitors.scale_or_funding: 750k+ registered humans; $2.1M+ paid out to workers (site claim)

competition.white_space:
Things I did not find. I could not run WebSearch (the session budget of 200 was used up), so this comes from Google News RSS queries and direct page fetches. I did not check Crunchbase, YC's directory, Product Hunt or GitHub in depth; a GitHub repository search returned nothing.

1. No funded company sells human-executed, ad hoc, arbitrary-protocol wet-lab work through an agent-native ticket API with a fixed price and a signed record separating AI proposal, human edit and physical execution. The nearest pieces are split across companies. Adaptyv has the agent API but runs standardized automated assays. CRO marketplaces have custom human work but run on quotes and SOWs. Transfyr has the execution-record capture but no labor. Emerald and Ginkgo have flexible automation but were not found to offer human-run ad hoc work to agents.
2. The long tail beyond fixed assays is the actual gap. That means multi-step, protocol-specific molecular biology that a robot cannot be programmed for in time: novel enzyme or nuclease activity validation, cloning plus cell-free expression plus a custom activity readout, and unusual cell-culture assays. Anthropic's post confirms this is where a frontier lab keeps human scientists.
3. Nobody I found sells biosafety-screened human execution of AI-proposed protocols as a service, even though oversight of AI-directed experiments is in the news (Lab Manager, 'Biosafety Oversight for AI-Directed Lab Experiments', Sept 28, 2026; Frontiers paper on automated-lab security tiers).

The window is narrow and closing.
- Adaptyv has $40M, agent-native positioning, a stated plan to add 'more complex biological workflows', and Chai and Boltz as customers. It can move toward the ad hoc tail with automation.
- Scientist.com and Science Exchange could add an agent API or MCP layer around their existing providers with modest effort.
- Transfyr could bundle records with any CRO.
- Anthropic and other frontier labs are insourcing bench capacity.

Risks to the idea's own claims:
- BioSpace headlines show layoffs are easing: August 2026 biopharma layoffs were about 500, down 90% year over year, and the Q2 job report says postings are rising. Skilled hands are still available, but the 'layoff wave' supply story is weakening (via https://news.google.com/rss/search?q=biotech+layoffs+2026+BioSpace+job+cuts+tracker).
- Sublet-bench operations carry insurance, contamination, quality-control and IP-chain-of-custody risk that a software-style API hides.
- The 35-45% gross margin at $1.5-8k per experiment is unproven against commodity CROs and against Adaptyv's automation, which starts at $149 per protein for screening-level binding.
competition.evidence_of_demand:
Demand for agent-orderable wet-lab validation is real. Demand for human-run ad hoc work, specifically as a paid service to agents, is plausible but not directly evidenced.

Evidence that AI-first teams pay for outsourced physical validation:
- Adaptyv raised a $40M Series A in Aug 2026. It has 100+ customers including AI-native labs Chai Discovery and Boltz plus Roche and Novo Nordisk, throughput is up 5x in a year, and it is tripling capacity. Its own stated endpoint is 'enough automated experimental capacity for AI to learn from physical reality as quickly as it learns from text' (https://www.startupticker.ch/en/news/adaptyv-raises-40m-to-build-automated-lab-for-agentic-biology; https://www.adaptyvbio.com/blog).
- Adaptyv ships an MCP server so Claude can order experiments (https://docs.adaptyvbio.com/llms.txt). Anthropic and Adaptyv launched a protein-design competition with 5,000+ experimental validations (Dealroom, Sept 22, 2026).
- Ginkgo lists 130+ customers for cloud lab and Datapoints services (https://www.ginkgo.bio/). OpenAI's GPT-5 ran 36,000 experiments in Ginkgo's cloud lab, and Ginkgo staff still handled reagents and consumables (https://www.rdworldonline.com/ginkgo-co-founder-reshma-shetty-on-autonomous-labs-ai-designed-experiments-and-the-human-side-of-the-equation/).
- Scientist.com cites $3B+ of scientific procurement activity and 6,000+ providers (https://www.scientist.com). This is existing spend on outsourced custom bench work.
- Benchling launched one-click ordering with Twist, Adaptyv and Ginkgo (PR Newswire, May 6, 2026).
- Funding is flowing into AI-lab infrastructure: Transfyr $25M seed, Medra $52M Series A, Lila and Periodic at multi-billion-dollar valuations (Google News RSS results).

Evidence that human bench work is the bottleneck the idea targets:
- Anthropic's Sept 2026 post says 'All of the lab work is performed by human scientists'. It says automation 'is less conducive to the sort of ad hoc workflows that are involved in our molecular biology research'. It also says 'If you have a proposal for a research question, we would like to hear from you' (https://www.anthropic.com/news/claude-discovers-novel-enzyme-system).
- The Stanford Virtual Biotech (37,000 agents) coverage is dated Sept 17-19, 2026. A Korea JoongAng Daily headline on Sept 22 reads 'AI drug race moves from finding candidates to proving they work'.
- OpenAI Foundation's Public Data for Health program gave $125M for biology data generation (Inside Precision Medicine and MIT Technology Review, Sept 15, 2026). That is grant-funded demand for data generation, though not specifically for outsourced human bench work.

Evidence gaps: I found no forum complaint, RFP or paying-customer example specifically for human-executed ad hoc experiments ordered by agents. I found no evidence of regulation forcing spend on execution records; Lab Manager's Sept 28 piece on biosafety oversight suggests the topic is emerging. The demand evidence is therefore mostly for adjacent, automated or CRO-based services.
competition.sharper_angle:
Do not build a general 'bench-for-hire API'. That collides with Adaptyv, which has $40M, an MCP server and a stated move into complex workflows, and with CRO marketplaces that could add an API in a quarter. Build the overflow and escalation tier that automated and catalog vendors cannot serve, and sell it with biosafety and provenance attached.

1. Narrow the scope to agent-discovered novel proteins, meaning enzymes, nucleases, reverse transcriptases and CRISPR-like systems, where the work is cloning plus cell-free or cell expression plus a bespoke activity readout. Robots do not have these protocols pre-programmed, and Anthropic's own post says it keeps humans at the bench for exactly this. Sell it first to AI-for-protein and agent-swarm startups, and to frontier-lab science teams that would rather subcontract than build more bench capacity.
2. Make the differentiator a human-executed, biosafety-screened, attested record. Each ticket gets a biosafety review of the AI-proposed protocol by a senior scientist. It returns a signed record separating AI proposal, human edit and physical execution, with raw data. This targets the unaddressed oversight gap (Lab Manager, Sept 28, 2026) and is something Adaptyv's automation-only positioning does not sell. It also gives frontier labs a compliance reason to route work to you.
3. Partner rather than compete on fixed assays. Route standard binding, expression and thermostability to Adaptyv or Ginkgo through their APIs and take only the tickets they reject or cannot express. Integrate with Transfyr-style capture instead of building sensors. That removes the commodity margin fight and turns the biggest competitors into a lead source.
4. Cut the sublet-bench plan. Start inside one or two existing CRO or shared labs (an incubator such as LabCentral or a partner CRO) with insurance, contamination control and IP chain of custody already in place. Use the laid-off scientists as a vetted contractor bench, but treat layoffs as a recruiting channel, not a growth thesis, since layoffs are easing.
5. Validate demand before building. Get 3 paid pilots from AI-protein startups and one frontier-lab science team at $1.5-8k per ticket, and test whether they pay a premium for the biosafety and provenance record. Anthropic's public invitation for outside research proposals is the first outreach target. If nobody pays a premium over what Adaptyv or a CRO charges, the idea collapses into a low-margin CRO and should be dropped.
